REFERENCE REGARDING THE FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF 
TERRORIST ATTACK ON THE PARLIAMENT BUILDING ON 
13TH DECEMBER, 2001 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, th is day, December 13, marks the 
first anniversary of the ghastly terrorist attack on the Parliament House building, 
which shocked not only the entire nation, but also the conscience of all peace 
loving people who cherish democratic values and ethos. It is undoubtedly the 
most audacious and alarming act of terrorism by rtain terrorist outfits who are 
inimical towards our country. The House „alls the heroic deed of our security 
personnel, including two of the -tajya Sabha Secretariat Watch and Ward staff, 
who made the superme crifice, along wi th five Delhi Police Personnel and a 
woman constable or CRPF, to thwart the entry of terrorists inside the 
Parliament House building. In the terrorist attack, one gardener of the CPWD 
also lost his life. We pay our respectful homage to them. Their dedication, 
devotion to duty and timely action had succeeded in averting what could have 
been a  lajo catastrophe. 
Terrorism should be condemned unambiguously. It can be defeated only 
through determination and sustained efforts. On this occasion, we resolve to 
fight terrorism unitedly and with determination tc eliminate it. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of those who lost their lives in that tragedy. 
[Honourable Members then stood in silence for one minute]

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Study of railway bridges 
*341. SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Railway staff study bridges abroad" published in the Times of 
India dated the 4th November, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether there was any proposal to send a Railways team 
abroad, to study inspection methods of bridges, as reported; 
(c) if so, whether any team was sent or is being sent; and 
(d) the justification for sending the team? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) to (d): 
A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) and (d) Upgradation of technology and modernisation of various 
systems is a continuous ongoing process of Indian Railways. As part of the 
process, presentations were arranged from various firms from abroad on modern 
bridge inspection and management systems. Many of the emerging areas of 
new technologies now being applied in areas like underwater inspection of 
bridges, non-destructive testing of bridges and bridge management systems 
were noted. A proposal to set up a task force to study the needs for upgrading 
and modernisation of bridge inspection and management systems especially 
underwater inspections and non-destructive testing of bridges was mooted in 
March, 2002. The task force was formally set up in September, 2002. Since 
techniques and equipment for such inspections are not available in the country, 
it was considered necessary to study their actual functioning abroad. As a part 
of the terms of reference of task force it was asked to visit countries abroad for 
on the spot study of the systems abroad. The team went abroad for the study tour 
on 3.11.2002 and returned on 28.11.2002.

Indian students in foreign universities 
*349. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any study has been conducted to analyse the problems 
increasingly faced by the larger nu mber of Indian students enrolling 
themselves in foreign universities for higher education and specialised 
courses; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the action taken/proposed to be taken to 
safeguard the interests of the student community, especially measures against 
bogus foreign universities? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(DR.MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
While no specific study on the problems of Indian students studying in 
foreign universities has been conducted by the Government according to the 
information compiled by the Association of Indian Universities on the basis of 
advertisements appearing in the Indian newspapers 144 foreign 
universities/colleges/institutions are offering various courses of study to the 
Indian students. With a view to safeguard the interests of the student 
community, the University Grants Commission has framed draft Regulations 
for regulating the entry into and operations of foreign universities/educational 
institutions in the country. Besides, the Government has constituted a 
Committee with the objective of regulating operations of foreign educational 
institutions in India. The Government 
28

has also taken up the matter with Indian Missions in major foreign countries, such as 
United States of America.Canada, United Kingdom, Australia and New 
Zealand, to check on the antecedents and credibility of educational institutions from 
these countries offering education to Indian students.

Boosting to Bio-Technology Sector 
*350. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the 
Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India is posing for phenomenal growth in Bio-
technology; 
(b) if so, what is the estimated potential of the country; and 
(c) what steps are being taken to give a boost to the Bio-technology 
sector? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The growth of biotechnology has been 
exponential in the last decade with various initiatives taken in public and private 
sector. India has enormous potential to utilize biotechnological tools for increasing 
the productivity and efficiency of agriculture, healthcare, environmental protection 
and industrial sectors. As per the estimates of Confederation of Indian Industry 
(CM), the actual consumption of biotech products during 1999 was about US$ 
1.78 billion and is projected to grow to US$ 4.27 billion by 2010. The biotech 
products in high demand are for human and animal healthcare, agriculture 
including genetically superior seeds, industry and other value added 
recombinant products. With the advent of bioinformatics, genomics and 
proteomics, it is estimated that the growth of this sector will be further 
accelerated covering almost every facet of life. 
Government of India has made concerted efforts to speed up research and 
development, application and commerciali zation of research leads. From Rs. 
622 crore in Ninth Plan (1997—2002), an outlay of Rs.1450 crore for the 
Tenth Plan (2002—07) has been allocated. Further impetus has been provided 
with the establishment of 62 bioinformatics centres, 25 state-of-the-art biotech 
facilities, Centres of Excellence and 64  postgraduate teaching programmes, 
establishment of a National Bioresource Development Board, new institutions 
like National Brain Research Centre, National Centre for Plant Genome Research 
and Institute of Bioresource and Sustainable Development in addition to many 
other national laboratories in frontier areas of biology and biotechnology. 
Significant achievements have been in obtaining research leads, transfer of 
technology, large scale demonstrations and commercialization of 
35 

RAJY ASABHA [13 December, 2002] 
products. Vaccines, diagnostic kits, drug delivery systems and bioremediation 
methods, tissue culture protocols, bio-fertilizers and biopesticides are at various 
stages of development and commercialization. 
To boost the biotech sector for the Biotech Product and Process 
Development, the Government has given various incentives to the biotech industry 
through fiscal measures, custom and ex cise duty exemptions, tax holidays for 
R&D expenditure, encouraging Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), speedy 
clearance of FDI projects by Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB), 
constitution of Fast Track Committee (FTC) under Foreign Investment 
Implementation Authority (FIIA) etc. To  inculcate biotech industry in small-
scale sector, a Task Force and a Biotec hnology Cell have been created in the 
Ministry of Small Scale Industries, Agro and Rural Industries in association 
with Department of Biotechnology. A sensitization programme in the form of 
workshops has jointly been initiated for awareness building in SSI 
entrepreneurs. 
State Governments have taken initiatives to establish biotechnology parks 
and incubators, separate biotech departments and institutes specially to focus on 
local problems. Successful mission projects with biotechnological 
interventions are under implementation in the areas of vaccines, coffee 
improvement, herbal product development and establishment of genomic 
databases. International collaboration has been strengthened with many developed 
and developing countries in the areas of mutual benefit. Research in new areas 
like nanobiology, structural and computational biology has also been initiated. 
The main objective of the above measures is to develop a strong capability in the 
field and harness the potential of biotechnology for societal benefit and economic 
progress.

*353.SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU):Will the Minister 
of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to ratify the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, 
for a time bound reduction of Green House Gases, responsible for global 
warming and climatic changes;

direction; 
(c) the steps taken by Government for reduction of green house gases, 
since 1997, so. far; and

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) India acceded to the Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations 
Framework Convention on Climate Change in August, 2002. The Kyoto Protocol 
commits developed countries to reduce their emissions of greenhouse gases by an 
average of 5.2% with reference to 1990 emission levels during the period 2008-
2012. It does not provide for similar emission reduction commitments for the 
developing countries. 
The steps taken by the Government to address greenhouse gas 
emissions include measures relating to energy efficiency, energy conservation, 
power sector reforms,renewable energy programmes, fuel switching to cleaner 
energy, afforestation and conservation of forests, efficient utilization of coal, 
reduction of gas flaring, installation of heat recovery system in oil and power 
sector, standardization of fuel efficient irrigation pump sets and better cultivar 
practices. These measures have, helped to increase energy efficiency, decrease 
pollution and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

denies meaningful market access to the developing countries; and depresses the 
international prices. In view of this in the negotiations on WTO Agreement on

forms of domestic support by the developed countries and elimination of 
export subsidies except export subsidies provided by all developing countries to 
reduce their high costs of marketing, including handling, upgrading and other 
processing costs; and costs of transport and freight, under Article 9.1 (d) and (e)

Melting of Glaciers of Himalayas 
  2396. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Is a blanket of smog chocking South Asia" appearing in the Times 
of India dated the 13th August, 2001; 
(b) if so, whether it is a fact that a recent study by the Delhi University in 
Kullu Valley has revealed that 67 per cent of the 1500 major Glaciers in the 
Himalayas are receding, which could resu lt in abrupt transition in climatic 
conditions, causing rise of 9.88 cm in sea level by 2100 and erosion of low 
lying areas; and 
(c) if so, what is Government's perception about this new phenomenon and the 
steps being contemplated, so that such a situation could be averted? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. An international collaborative study namely, "Indian 
Ocean Research Experiment (INDOEX)" has indicated haze over the Indian Ocean. 
The haze is not a permanent feature of the atmosphere over the Asian region and 
the surrounding seas. It occurs only during January -March, the season in 
which INDOEX observations were made in 1999. The United Nations 
Environment Programme (UNEP) has, this year, brought out a report entitled 
"The Asian Brown Cloud: Climate and other Environmental Impacts" based on 
INDOEX. The press release of the UNEP launching the said report paints an 
alarming picture of the impacts of this baze on both regional and global scales. 
However, most of the concerns expressed therein are not well substantiated by 
reliable modeling studies or experimental observations. 
79 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
(b) The University of Delhi has conducted studies in Kullu Valley on land 
use patterns and not on blanket of smog or on the recession of Himalayan 
Glaciers, sea level rise and erosion of low lying areas. However, according to the 
Geological survey of India, as per the inventory of Himalayan Glaciers, the 
Indian part of Himalaya has more than 7500 glaciers of all dimensions. There 
are only 365 major glaciers more than 5 km in length (excluding Shyok and 
Kishanganga basins). The studies conducted by the Survey reveal that the 
majority of them are receding. The rate of recession in different climate zones of 
Himalaya is found to be variable in different years. Therefore, the studies 
confine to Kullu Valley may not give the overall natural cyclic process. The 
earth has witnessed several phases of glacial and interglacial period. It is a natural 
phenomenon. Presently the earth is passing through an interglacial phase whereby 
the ice bodies throughout the world are receding and the recession of glacier is a 
natural phenomenon and could also be attributed to global warming. 
(c) Regarding smog, it may be mentioned that the existing legal and policy 
framework supported by several initiatives to protect and improve the 
environment, addresses the concerns of air pollution in India. Regarding recession 
of the Himalayan Glaciers, the Govern ment is aware of the environmental 
concerns and has supported conservation activities in the Himalayan region 
including afforestation, establishment of community toilets, and removal of 
garbage and promotion of eco-tourism.

BAALU): (a) No, Sir. Faulty land use, developmental activities, geo-
morphological changes and loss of vegetal cover are some of the factors 
responsible for drying up of water sources in hilly regions.

outer and middle Himalayas and to some extent in the inner Himalayas upto 
the elevation of 1800 mts. and their distribution depends upon the edaphic and

invasion of pines in the areas of broad-leaved species. Preference is given to the

no longer a priority species in the plantation programmes undertaken in the 
region.

BAALU): (a) and (b) Yes Sir; The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee 
(GEAC) accorded conditional clearance for introduction of three Bt. cotton 
hybrids namely BT MECH 162, BT MECH 184, BT MECH 12 into the 
environment for a period of three years from April 2002 to March 2005. The 
conditions, inter-alia, include plantation of a non-Bt refuge around the periphery 
of the Bt fields equivalent to five rows of non_Bt cotton variety or 20% of the 
total sown area, monitoring the susceptibility of bollworms to Bt gene vis-a-vis 
baseline susceptibility data by an agency identified by the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests, undertaking studies on possible impacts on non-target 
insects and crops, developing plans for Bt based Integrated Pest Management, 
developing and depositing with the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Research 
(NBPGR), the DNA fingerprints of the 
84 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
approved varieties and undertaking of an awareness and education

in six states namely Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Some of the fields where these hybrid 
varieties are being cultivated have recently been monitored by the Committees 
constituted by this Ministry for each state. The Committees found the 
performance of Bt. Cotton satisfactory.

seeds in India.

held on 7th November, 2002 considered the proposal but no final decision was

gene (s), biochemical characterization of the expressed proteins, estimation of 
level of expressed proteins, safety of the expressed proteins to the non-target 
organisms, environmental fate of expressed proteins, pollen escape, 
outcrossing, aggressiveness and weediness, effect on non-target organisms, 
confirmation of the absence of Terminator Gene, and baseline susceptibility 
studies and agronomic, compositional and food and feed safety evaluation of 
transgenic hybrids as compared to the non-transgenic counterpart.

Trading of Indian Saras 
2419. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of ENVIORNMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that trading of Indian Saras, the State bird of Uttar 
Pradesh, is prohibited under the Wildlife Protection Act; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that there are only 8000 Saras all over the 
world, of which 6000 are in Uttar Pradesh, but these are much on sale in the 
market of Lucknow; and 
(c) if so, what steps are being taken by Government to rescue the bird, 
for conservation? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, sir. 
(b) and (c) As per the survey report of Wildlife Institute of India, the 
estimated total population of Saras in the world is 8000-10,000, out of which 
about 4000-5000 birds are in Uttar Pradesh .There have been media reports 
regarding sale of Saras in the market of Lucknow but these have not been 
confirmed on investigation. However, to prevent any sale of Saras cranes 
constant vigil is kept by the field staff.

Commercial production of GM Mustard 
†2422. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHAR DA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any proposal to permit Genetically Modified (GM) Mustard, 
prepared by mixing five types of foreign genes, for commercial production, is 
under Government's consideration; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
113 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) by when a final decision in this regard is likely to be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) No, Sir. The transgenic hybrid mustard developed by M/s. 
Proagro Seed Company Ltd. for improving the yield contain three genes for 
three traits; these are (i) bar (glucosinolate ammonium tolerance trait), (ii) bamase 
(male sterility producing trait), and (iii) barstar (restoration of fertility trait). Based 
on the recommendation of the Monitoring-cum-Evaluation Committee (MEC) 
of the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and Review Committee on Genetic 
Manipulation (RCGM), the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) 
in its 27th Meeting held on 8th August, 2001 permitted M/s. Proagro Seeds 
Company Ltd. to conduct large scale open field trials. Subsequently the 
Company submitted the proposal for approval of the GEAC for commercial 
release and marketing of transgenic mustard and seed production.The GEAC has 
not given the approval as yet. 
GM Mustard 
2423. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN:            
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have given approval for genetically modified 
mustard being marketed in the country; 
(b) if so, whether an evaluation has been made of the benefits of higher 
productivity vis-a-vis the risks to health and local varieties; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether the insect-resistant Bt. Cotton crop has been found to be 
successful; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) 
114 

 
[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
in its 27th Meeting held on 8th August, 2001 permitted M/s. Proagro Seeds 
Company Ltd. Gurgaon to conduct large scale open field trials only. The 
company has been involved in the research and development of transgenic hybrids 
of Indian mustard for improving the yield for the last three years, following 
Department of Biotechnology guidelines. During the field trials the hybrids 
have been tested and compared with the non-transgenic hybrid for various 
parameters. It has been found that the hybrids offered better agronomic 
performance over the best available varieties in the country. Subsequently, the 
request of the company to allow for commercial release and marketing of 
transgenic mustard and seed production was considered by the GEAC in the 34th 
Meeting held on 7th November, 2002.The GEAC has decided to further examine 
the data submitted by the company.

Admission in engineering and medical science studies 
2436. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that non-Government institutions, 
conducting professional courses generally take huge amount from the 
124 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
students seeking admission in engineering and medical science studies; 
(b) what sort of control Government are maintaining over such 
institutions; 
(c) whether Government are planning to increase the in-take capacity of 
Government sponsored professional colleges, to admit students in more number; 
and 
(d) if so, the details of such plants? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (d) 
Engineering Education 
The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) has constituted 
various State Level Fee Committees for fixing Fees to be charged by self-
financing technical institutions. The State level fee committee consist of Vice 
Chancellor of a University in the Stat e, Secretaries of the Department of 
Technical Education and Department of Finance, two economist or experts in 
cost accountancy with back ground of institutional finance and Member 
Secretary not below the rank of Joint Secretary or director of the State 
Government. All the self-financing institutions are bound by the fees structure 
prescribed by the Fee Committees and ar e not allowed to charge excess fees, 
capitation fees or donation for the purpose of admission from the students. The 
concerned state government are supposed to monitor the technical institutions. 
Whenever such cases of overcharging of the fees and collection of capitation 
and donations from the students come to the notice of the AICTE, appropriate 
actions are taken against such institutions after conducting necessary 
investigations into such matters. 
2. Technical institutions are expected to follow norms and standards 
prescribed by the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE). This also 
includes fees structure prescribed by State Level Fee Committees. If a technical 
institution does not do so, punitive acti on such as putting it under 'Reduced 
Intake' or 'No Admission' category may be taken. 
3. AICTE has not made any plan for increase in intake for Government aided 
Professional Colleges in technical education. However, if a technical institution 
submits application to AICTE for increase in intake of seats 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
the same is considered by AICTE as per laid down procedure and norms & 
standards. 
Medical Science 
1. With a view to prevent the commercialization of medical colleges, and 
also to prevent private medical colleges from charging capitation fees, the 
Supreme Court of India in the Case of Unnikrishnan J.R versus State, evolved a 
scheme for regulating admissions in private medical colleges. As per the 
scheme, 50% of the total seats are to be merit seats, 35% payment seats and the 
remaining 15% earmarked for NRI/Foreign students in all the private medical 
colleges, except for minority colleges. The admission fo the first two categories 
i.e. merit and payment seats is to be made by the competent authority in the 
respective States, on the basis of merit to be determined either on the basis of a 
competitive entrance test or the merit determined in the qualifying examination. 
In minority medical colleges, 50% seats are filled through the competent 
authority of the respective State Government and remaining 50% filled by the 
management on the basis of merit amongst the candidates belonging to the 
concerned minority. Since merit is the sole criteria for obtaining admissions, 
hard-working and meritorious students have benefited by the scheme evolved by 
the Supreme Court. As regards the fee st ructure, this had been fixed by the 
Supreme Court for the period 1993-94 to 1996-97. Subsequently, the Central 
Government has been fixing the upper ceiling of the fee for merit and payment 
seats in private medical college and within this upper ceiling, the fees in each 
medical college is being fixed by the respective State Government. No fee has. 
however, been prescribed by the Central Government for 15% seats earmarked 
for NRI/Foreign students. The eleven Judge Bench of Supreme Court of India had 
recently given a judgment on admission and fee in aided and unaided medical 
institution. 
2. At present there is no proposal to increase the intake capacity. 
However, any applicant fulfilling the eligibility and qualifying criteria 
prescribed in the regulations "The Opening of a New or Higher Course of Study or 
Training (including Post-graduate Course of Study or Training) and Increase of 
Admission Capacity in any Course of Study or Training (including a Post-
graduate Course of Study or Training) Regulations, 2000" brought out by the 
Medical Council of India, can apply for permission to 
126 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the Central Government for increase  in admission capacity in medical 
colleges.

funding by the University Grants Commission; and

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMAJ: (a) Yes,

observations: 
"The UGC has responsibility for extending assistance for both standards

UGC, the share of research is a small fraction. Apart from other equally 
valid reasons, this situation is also responsible for universities steadily 
losing primacy in the R&D effort in the country."

(b)The major recommendations ma de by the Expenditure Reforms 
Commission in its recent report, inter-alia, are: (i) there is a need to develop in-
house academic expertise in the UGC, (ii) the responsibility for determination 
and disbursement of maintenance grant to Delhi Colleges should be transferred 
along with the funds to the appropri ate agency designated by the State 
Government of Delhi, (iii) there is a need to review a large number of programmes 
initiated by UGC so as to ensure that the meager funds available with the UGC 
are not thinly spread over a large number of activities, (iv) UGC should seek to 
enhance the resources to be allocated for 'research' out of the total funds and find 
better means to optimally utilize these funds by devising result-oriented 
approach and (v) UGC should take steps to promote the quality in the 
universities and colleges and establish linkages between the accreditation of the 
institutions with the release of the grants etc.

for the increased funding in research. However, the disbursement of grants to the 
universities and colleges for different programmes, including research projects 
depends on the quantum of funds made available to the UGC. Despite the 
financial constraints the research has been a prime concern of the UGC. The

Pre-Harappan civilization 
2465. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of OCEAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that National Institute of Ocean Technology had 
indicated a likely Pre-Harappan civilization; 
(b) if so, what is the basis for the exploration; and 
(c) what further steps have been taken to conduct research in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF OCEAN DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b)The Natio nal Institute of Ocean Technology 
(NIOT), Chennai of the Department of Ocean Development (DOD) 
Government of India had during the course of under water surveys in the Gulf of 
Cambay, Gujarat during Cctober, 2000 to March, 2001 come across a stretch of 
formations typical of a riverine regime in the middle of the sea at 30—40 m. 
water depth. An area of almost 9km. Stretch west of Hazira in Gujarat appeared 
to be lined with well laid house basement like feature 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2002] 
partially covered by sand waves and sand ripples. The Side Scan Sonar deployed 
for the survey picked up images which indicate several geometric objects that are 
normally man made. 
During subsequent surveys in November-December, 2001 various objects 
were picked up from the sea bed. Among the objects collected, the carbonized 
wood pieces were taken up for dating using C14 technique in the Birbal Sahni 
Institute of Palaeo Botany, Lucknow and in National Geophysical Research 
Institute, Hyderabad. The preliminary results reveal that the age of the w ood 
samples dated back to 7500 B.C. This has been further substantiated by dating 
carried out at laboratories in Germany. 
These results and some of the objects collected were made public in a 
Press Conference on 16th January, 2002. Further detailed surveys, studies and 
investigations would need to be done in the area by multi-disciplinary, multi-
institutional teams to conclusively establish the period of settlement. 
(c) As a follow up, a workshop was organized on 1 st July 2002 at NIOT 
campus, Chennai which was attended by about 50 eminent personalities 
belonging to different fields like archaeology, geology, geo-morphology, geo-
chronology and marine technology. Based on the recommendations in the 
workshop, several organisations and institutions were asked to give proposal 
pertaining to the expertise that will be of importance to the gulf of Cambay 
marine archeological findings.

2466. SHRI R.P. GOEN KA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Commissioners of Railway Safety, who 
conduct inquiries into major rail accidents, cannot function independently and 
impartially, as they are dependent on the Ministry of Railways for all their 
important requirements, like office and residential accommodation, transport 
and other perks for their officers, as well as for submitting their findings on 
accidents to the Railway board; 
(b) if so, the details of the review undertaken, if any, to ensure an 
independent statutory authority status for the Chief Commissioner of Railway 
Safety; and 
156 

[13 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the comparative set up obtaining in some other countries like 
Britain, USA etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) The Commissioners of Railway Safety, 
whose one of the many functions is to conduct inquiries into serious rail 
accidents, are entitled to get infrastructure support viz. accommodation, 
transport, etc. from the Ministry of Railways. They are, however, independent 
of the Ministry of Railways as their budget, appointment, promotion, pay & 
allowances etc. are under the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The fac ilities being 
provided by the Railways are as per the service conditions agreed by the 
Ministry of Railways.They function independently and impartially in conducting 
accident inquiries and finalising their reports. 
The accident inquiry reports are fina lly submitted to the Ministry of 
Railways, as the Railway Board is the safety controlling authority and they 
examine and implement the accepted recommendations, made by the 
Commissioners. 
(b) Railway Safety Review Committee (1998) has also supported the 
independent nature and status of the Commission of Railway Safety. 
(c) In USA, National Transport Safety Board (NTSB) is an independent 
Federal agency charged with investig ation in every major accident of all 
transportation sectors. In Britain, the functions of Railway Safety Inspectorate 
called the "Her Majesty's Safety Inspector ate" are broadly similar to that of 
Commission of Railway Safety in India.

SHRI U.V. KRISHNAM RAJU: Sir, concerns have been raised by 
hon. Members in regard to the poisonous effects on wheat, rice, sugar and 
other food items on being packed in plastic bags for a long duration of time. 
It may be recalled that the Government of India have approved the 
road map for dilution of the compulsory packaging norms laid down under the 
Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 
1987 in respect of foodgrains in July 2002. This has been done with a view to 
enabling the jut® industry to become cost and quality competitive in domestic 
and international markets. The cumulative percentages of dilution for 
foodgrains for the Jute Year (July to June) 2002-2003 and 2003-2004 are 20% 
and 40% respectively. The percentages of reservation for packaging in jute 
bags will, therefore, be 80% and 60% for foodgrains for the 1 st and 2 nd year 
respectively. The position will be reviewed in the 3rd year. 
The Indian Grain Storage Managem ent and Research Institute 
(IGSMRI), Hapur, a research and development institution of the Department of 
Food and Public Distribution has conduc ted a scientific stud y to evaluate the 
suitability of PP/HDPE bags for the storage of foodgrains under field 
conditions. The study was conducted in different agro-climatic zones at Food 
Storage' Depots (FSD) of the Food Corporation of India (FCI) situated at Delhi, 
Shahjahanpur (UP). Cherlapally & Samalkot (AP), Kollam (Kerala), 
Bhubaneswar (Orissa), Jallandhar (Punjab), Una (HP), Rampur (MP) and 
Jorhat (Assam) for different commodities like wheat and rice. 
On the basis of the study, the IGSMRI has found that: 
(I)    PP/ HDPE bags are light in weight as compared to jute bags. 
00   PP/ HDPE bags are cheaper as compared to jute bags. 
(iii)   Prophylactic and curative treatment against stored grain insect 
pests is effective. 
The IGSMRI conducted its res earch study for one year storage 
period and has recommended that: 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December, 2003] 
"PP/HDPE antislip bags can be used for storage of foodgrains by 
State procuring agencies in a phased ma nner, preferably to begin with the 
operational stocks in covered godowns at safe moisture level". 
The Indian Institute of Technolo gy (IIT), New Delhi has also 
conducted studies on the use of PP/HDPE bags for packaging of foodgrains 
and other items and found that Plastic Woven Sacks (PWS) made of HDPE or 
PP outperform their traditional counter parts (jute and paper bags) due to 
superiority exhibited in the following key functional areas : 
Low seepage loss, yet option of breathing requirement not sacrificed. 
Moisture resistant: hence most suitable packaging for hygroscopic 
substances like, fertilizer and sugar. 
Water and insect resistant, thus allowing the PP-HDPE bags to be 
stored in warehouses and godowns wi thout fear of deterioration and 
subsequent wastage. 
The Indian Council of Medical Rese arch (ICMR) on the basis of a 
study conducted by the National Institut e of Nutrition (NIN), Hyderabad has 
indicated that, as per available informat ion, food items like grains and flours 
can be safely stored in plastic bags. However, conditions like initial moisture 
content, inoculum potential of biolog ical agents like insects and fungi, 
conditions of storage including temp erature and humidity, surrounding 
hygiene, and frequency of fumigation ha ve considerable bearing on the 
stability of the product and these vary according to the type of agricultural 
commodity. 
The Bureau of Indian Standards  (BIS) has standardised the 
specifications of PP / HDPE woven sacks for packaging of foodgrains and 
sugar. The BIS have indicated that the standards on HDPE/PP bags for 
packing of foodgrains and sugar have been issued after due consideration of 
health and safety aspects. The packaging of cereals and sugar is governed by 
the various BIS specifications, wherein the requirement of the overall migration 
limit (combination of all those constitu ents which adversely affect health) has 
been prescribed. It has, inter alia, been prescribed that foodgrains and sugar 
should be packed only in woven sacks made of

specific materials, which are reasonably safe for personal health. The BIS 
specifications of textiles - High De nsity Poly Ethyelene (HDPE) / Poly 
Propylene (PP) woven sacks for packaging foodgrains and sugar (No. IS 
14887 : 2000 & 14968 : 2001) prescribes that the raw material for the tape 
shall be manufactured from virgin High Density Poly Ethyelene (HDPE) / Poly 
Propylene (PP) conforming to requirements specified in IS: 10146 or IS: 10910 
respectively. The BIS have stated that  the aforesaid Indian Standards on 
plastic raw materials for use in contact with food items are based on 
internationally accepted requirements such as European Norms, US PDA 
Regulations. British Plastic Federation Report, London etc. on the subject. The 
BIS have further informed that for ensur ing quality of bags in terms of long 
term stability to prevent degradation durin g use, the use of UV stabilized raw 
materials has been specified in the standards listed in the above 
specifications. 
As per available information, PP bags for packing of sugar are being 
used in Indonesia. Malaysia, Middle East, Brazil, Cuba, and E.U. countries. 
The Directorate General of Health  Services have intimated that 
plastic bags manufactured out of the plastic packaging materials enlisted 
under Rule 49(5)(v) of Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules. 1955 are 
safe to pack foodgrains and sugar if the material used for manufacturing 
HDPE / PP bags conforms to the specifications prescribed by BIS. 
It may be mentioned that PP/HDPE woven sacks are produced from 
the same raw materials which are used in items of daily human consumption 
(in India as well as in other countries) such as milk, edible oils, consumer packs 
of rice, sugar, wheat, tea, coffee, flour, salt, spices and pulses. The items most 
sensitive to human health, such as medicines, life saving drugs, blood and 
plasma pouches are all packed in articles of PP/HDPE and other plastic raw 
materials. No report or incidence of poisonous effect of PP/HDPE bags during 
storage of foodgrains has so far come to Government's notice. 
In the light of the facts mentio ned above, health hazards do not 
appear to be involved in the use of PP/HDPE bags for packing of foodgrains 
and sugar. The Food Corporation of India (FCI) is yet to take decision   on
